name: Kukuruku
confidence_why: Strub's 1915-1916 grammar, the only description of Kukuruku (Etsako) that mentions stress at all, places the dynamic accent almost always on the first syllable alongside three tones and repeats that placement for derived nouns and compounds, and nothing contradicts it, though Laver 1967 and Elimelech 1976 describe the language purely as a tone language and never mention stress.

new_statements.translation: b) A dot on a vowel or to the right of a vowel marks the place of the dynamic accent [= stress]. Since this is almost always on the first syllable, it will be marked only in the cases which are exceptions to this rule. — 4. Tonal accents. In Kukuruku there are three tonal accents: the high tonal accent, marked ´; the low tonal accent, marked `; the rising tonal accent, marked ˇ. A vowel without a sign is short and has the mid tonal accent [...] (p. 452). — [...] the verb root receives a low tonal accent; the dynamic accent is generally placed on the first syllable. (p. 889, §37). Bracketed letters restore line-ends clipped in the scan's right margin.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is tonal (Strub: three marked tones high, low, rising, plus unmarked mid; modern sources: two underlying tones, five surface pitches). Separately from tone, Strub reports a 'dynamic accent' (stress) that falls almost always on the first syllable of the word, marked in his notation only when it falls elsewhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. Ch. VIII §34A (p. 888) states that within one word there can never be two dynamic accents on two consecutive syllables, and in two-word combinations either word may keep or lose its stress under vowel elision; §34B lists the four possible stress placements in pairs of bisyllabic words (first or second syllable of each).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with stress off the first syllable exist and are marked with a dot (p. 452); elision and euphony suppress 'a certain number of encumbering dynamic accents' and modify tones in connected speech (p. 888, §34); in combinations b-d of bisyllabic words the stress may sit on the second syllable of a word (p. 888); §37 says 'généralement' (generally) rather than 'always' for deverbal nouns (p. 889).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('accent dynamique' = stress vs 'accent tonique' = tone), with phrase-level adjustments described for two-word combinations (Ch. VIII). Missionary description (Société des Missions Africaines de Lyon) of 'Kukuruku' = the Wano dialect of Agenigbodi/Agenebode (Weppa-Wano clan) per Thomas 1910: 143. The modern descriptions (Laver 1967, Elimelech 1976/1978) are silent on stress and treat the language as purely tonal, so Strub's stress claim is unconfirmed by later work.
new_statements.identity_note: Strub's 'Kukuruku' is, per Thomas 1910: 143 ('the Wano language (Agenigbodi) derived from Father Strub'), the Weppa-Wano dialect of Etsako spoken at Agenebode — a dialect of Yekhee (yekh1238), not a separate language. Laver 1967 describes the Aviele (Ayele) dialect near Agbede; Elimelech 1976/1978 focuses on Ekpheli with data from eight dialects. All fall under yekh1238; Glottolog gives no separate dialect codes that I saw.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (initial stress = initial stress) and as the existing statement (which quotes p. 452 §3(b)-§4). Adds that the language has three tone accents alongside the dynamic accent, that the initial placement is 'almost always' with marked exceptions, that derived nouns also take initial dynamic accent (p. 889 §37), and the compound/elision rules of p. 888 §34 (no two consecutive stressed syllables in a word). pp. 450-451 (contents, §1 vowels, §2 consonants) newly scanned: no accent statement there.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kukuruku has three lexical tones (high, low, rising, plus an unmarked mid) and, separately, a dynamic (stress) accent that falls almost always on the first syllable of the word; only exceptional placements are marked (with a dot). Derived nouns likewise generally carry the dynamic accent on the first syllable (§37). In noun+noun combinations with elision the dynamic accents of the two members interact: no two consecutive syllables may both be stressed, and the accent stays on the word the speaker wants to bring out (§34).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. §34 treats sequences of two words each with its own dynamic accent (four combinations of first/second-syllable accent) and states that within a single word two consecutive syllables cannot both carry a dynamic accent; when elision joins two nouns one accent may be suppressed or transferred.
new_statements.exceptions: 'presque toujours' / 'généralement' on the first syllable: exceptions exist and are marked with a dot in the orthography (p. 452); §34-35 describe suppression and substitution of dynamic accents in compounds and elided noun sequences (e.g. accent kept on the word to be emphasized; in frequently used numeral compounds the eliding vowel takes over the accents of the elided vowel).
new_statements.identity_note: Strub's 'Kukuruku' is the Weppa-Wano (Agenigbodi) variety of Etsako/Yekhee (Thomas 1910 preface and Appendix A; Elimelech 1976 p. 1 lists Weppa-Wano among the 13 Etsako clan dialects and identifies Strub's Kukuruku with Etsako). Elimelech 1976/1978 focuses on the Ekpheli dialect with comparative data from seven other clan dialects (Avianwu, Weppa-Wano, Uzairue, South Uneme, South Ibie, Auchi, Aviele); Laver 1967 describes the Aviele (Ayele) dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Elimelech, Baruch. 1976. A Tonal Grammar of Etsako. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 35 (August 1976), xiii+170 pp. [= UCLA PhD dissertation; revised as UC Publications in Linguistics 87, 1978].
tone_statements.quote: In 1911 I recorded with the help of Father Strub, of the Roman Catholic Mission, Agenebode, Southern Nigeria, six Yoruba and three Kukuruku songs, as nearly as they can be represented by our notation, and also the normal rise and fall of the tones in the spoken words. ... I had not at the time realised that the intermediate tones between high and low were so numerous. ... The small numbers above the vowels show the tones — 1 is high, 4 low.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Speech tones written 1 (high) to 4 (low) over Kukuruku song texts; no toneme count here. His 'Notes on Kukuruku' (Man 17 art. 32) gives four tones high, high-mid, low-mid, low.

tone_statements.citation: Elimelech, Baruch. 1974. Tone alternations in the Etsako verb. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 27: 63-73.
tone_statements.quote: While all verbs fall within one tone class, the exact phonological representation of this verb class is not obvious. For example, in (1a) the verb has a falling tone in the past tense and the customary tense but a low in the present tense. It has a high tone in (1b) in all constructions. ... I have given all of the possible tone classes of bisyllabic and trisyllabic nouns for reference as in (2). It should be noted that all nouns end in a low tone in Etsako. (2) Tone classes of bi- and tri-syllabic nouns: H-L : úkpò 'cloth' L-L : àkpà 'cup' H-H-L ... H-L-L ... L-L-L ... L-H-L : àtásà 'plate'
tone_statements.locator: pp. 63-64, introduction and ex. (2); see also p. 72: 'The language does not permit rising tones in lexical morphemes.'
tone_statements.summary: H vs L levels; rising/falling derived by contraction; no toneme count stated. Downstep only in notation (dá'tásà, 'LHL > H'HL'). Forms count is a floor. Argues all-L nouns carry one word-level L.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another on placement. Strub 1915/16 is the only source that states a word-stress rule (dynamic accent almost always initial, alongside three tones). Elimelech's 1976 version of A Tonal Grammar of Etsako (full text scanned, 180 pp) and Laver 1967 (already held by the project) describe Etsako as a tone language and never mention stress, accent or prominence; that is silence, not a denial of Strub's dynamic accent, but it means the initial-stress claim rests on one 1915 missionary description. Thomas 1910's 'dynamic accent normally on the penultimate' belongs to the Edo/Bini section of that report, not to Kukuruku (noted in our earlier reading), so it is not a conflict for yekh1238.

tone.quote: While all verbs fall within one tone class, the exact phonological representation of this verb class is not obvious. For example, in (1a) the verb has a falling tone in the past tense and the customary tense but a low in the present tense. It has a high tone in (1b) in all constructions. ... I have given all of the possible tone classes of bisyllabic and trisyllabic nouns for reference as in (2). It should be noted that all nouns end in a low tone in Etsako. (2) Tone classes of bi- and tri-syllabic nouns: H-L : úkpò 'cloth' L-L : àkpà 'cup' H-H-L ... H-L-L ... L-L-L ... L-H-L : àtásà 'plate'
tone.locator: pp. 63-64, introduction and ex. (2); see also p. 72: 'The language does not permit rising tones in lexical morphemes.'
tone.summary: H vs L levels; rising/falling derived by contraction; no toneme count stated. Downstep only in notation (dá'tásà, 'LHL > H'HL'). Forms count is a floor. Argues all-L nouns carry one word-level L.
